passage: I remember the night before my scholarship interview. My cousin Yamini poked her head in and said, brightly, "Relax, Ramesh, it will be fine!" and went back to her show. I felt something close inside me. Nobody had asked what I was afraid of. I nodded and said okay, but I stopped practising for an hour. Two weeks later, before my driving test, she sat next to me and said the same three words, quietly, after asking what worried me most. That time they helped. It made me see the words are not the thing; the tone and whether she wanted to hear me are. I wonder if she even noticed the difference.

qa.q: When was Yamini's bright "it will be fine"?
qa.a: It was the night before Ramesh's scholarship interview.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh feel something close inside him when Yamini said it?
qa.a: He felt she was not taking his fear seriously, since she did not ask what he was afraid of and went back to her show. He still nodded politely, so it was not obvious to her.

qa.q: What could Yamini do next time to make her comfort land better?
qa.a: Ask what worries him first, sit close and say the words quietly, as she did before the driving test.

qa.q: How might Yamini have seen her own remark that night?
qa.a: She may have thought she was cheering him up and had no idea it felt hollow.

grounding: The same words of reassurance comfort or dismiss depending on tone and timing.

passage: Counsellor's note, Friday. Suraj told me that after his maths exam he said he was afraid he had failed. His mother replied quickly, "Don't be silly, it will be fine," while packing his lunchbox. He nodded, but he told me the words felt like a door closing. He was not looking for a promise, he said, just for someone to ask which question troubled him. He also said his uncle's "It will be fine" felt good last month, because his uncle sat with him first and asked what happened. We talked about how he can say, "Can you listen first?" I have suggested he try telling his mother that. Naveen.

qa.q: What was Suraj's mother doing when she said it would be fine?
qa.a: She was packing his lunchbox.

qa.q: What did Suraj seem to want when he told his mother he might have failed?
qa.a: He seems to want someone to ask which question troubled him and to listen before comforting him. The words felt to him like a door closing.

qa.q: What could Suraj try with his mother?
qa.a: He could tell her plainly, "Can you listen first?" so she knows what helps him.

qa.q: How might Suraj's mother feel about his reaction?
qa.a: She may be surprised, since she meant to comfort him and did not intend to dismiss him.

grounding: Reassurance such as it will be fine can feel hollow to a teen depending on timing and tone.

passage: When I was sixteen, Harsha, I lent my friend's cricket bat to a boy and it came back cracked. My face burned, because Bala was captain and I didn't want to look small. So I made a joke: "Well, it's got character now!" Everyone laughed except Bala. I sent him a funny picture of a broken bat that evening, hoping he'd forget. He didn't reply for days. Finally my grandfather, your great-grandfather, said, "A joke isn't a sorry, Uday." I went to Bala's house and said, "I broke your bat. I'm sorry. I'll pay for a new one." Short, plain. He nodded and said, "Thanks. That's what I wanted." It cost me less than the joke.

qa.q: What happened to Bala's cricket bat?
qa.a: It came back cracked after being lent to a boy.

qa.q: Why did Uday joke and send a funny picture instead of apologising?
qa.a: He was embarrassed and afraid of looking small in front of the captain, so he tried to make it into something light. It seems that apologising felt like losing status.

qa.q: What did Uday do that finally repaired things?
qa.a: He went to Bala's house, said plainly that he broke the bat, said sorry and offered to pay for a new one.

qa.q: How might Bala have felt when the joke and picture came?
qa.a: He may have felt brushed off or annoyed, since the joke did not acknowledge what happened.

grounding: A teen avoids apologising to save face with jokes, and a short plain acknowledgement repairs the relationship.

passage: The bus to the football ground was leaving in ten minutes and Yogesh's phone buzzed twice. Dhruv, angry, had written: 'You forgot the plan again.' Yogesh had promised to bring the ball and left it at home. His first thought was a meme of a sad cat with the caption 'my bad lol'. He typed it, hovered, and deleted it. On the noisy platform, with shouting all around, he typed instead, 'I forgot the ball. That was on me, I'm sorry. I'll run home and get it and meet you at the ground.' Dhruv answered after a minute: 'ok. thanks for saying it.' Yogesh let out a breath. It didn't feel small at all.

qa.q: What had Yogesh forgotten to bring?
qa.a: He forgot to bring the ball.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh delete the meme before sending it?
qa.a: He probably sensed the joke would sound like he was avoiding the mistake, and he wanted to own it. The pull toward a joke shows how uncomfortable apologising felt.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do next after his apology?
qa.a: He can follow through on what he offered, going home for the ball and meeting Dhruv at the ground.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt on reading the plain apology?
qa.a: He probably felt heard and less angry, which is why he wrote 'thanks for saying it'.

grounding: A teen avoids a face-saving joke and gives a short plain apology.

passage: Our neighbour's daughter Noor was crying on the steps last week, and it reminded me of something, Imran. When I was young, my brother Anil said, "I'm sorry you feel that way," after he read my diary. I felt worse, because it sounded like it was my fault for being upset. I stopped speaking to him for a week. Years later I made the same mistake with my own son, saying, "Sorry, but you also left the door open." I saw him go still. I said, "Wait. I'm sorry I read your letter. No but. It was wrong of me." His shoulders came down. Listen for the 'but', beta. A real apology has nothing hanging on the end.

qa.q: What did Anil say after he read the narrator's diary?
qa.a: He said, "I'm sorry you feel that way."

qa.q: Why did the narrator feel worse after Anil's apology?
qa.a: It sounded as if being upset was her own fault, so she felt blamed rather than heard. She was hurt enough to stop speaking to him for a week.

qa.q: What did the narrator learn to do differently?
qa.a: She learned to say sorry for the act itself and drop the 'but'.

qa.q: How might Anil have felt about his own words?
qa.a: He may have thought he was apologising, without noticing how it sounded. 🙂

grounding: A conditional apology sounds like blame shifting, and an apology without excuses works better.

passage: The school canteen was deafening, plates clattering and a match blaring from the TV. Hrithik leaned across the table and shouted, "Sorry, but you also ignored my messages!" Tejas heard the word 'but' clearly. He put down his samosa. Was this an apology or a complaint dressed up? His neck felt warm, though he kept his voice level. "I'll answer for my part. But can you say the sorry part without the 'also'?" Hrithik blinked. "Okay. I'm sorry I said your project was boring. That was unkind." He paused. "And I still felt ignored." Tejas nodded. "Thank you. Let's talk about that one properly outside." They took their trays to the corridor, where it was quiet.

qa.q: Where were Tejas and Hrithik when Hrithik shouted his apology?
qa.a: They were in the noisy school canteen.

qa.q: What might Tejas have felt when he heard Hrithik say sorry but you also?
qa.a: He felt his neck get warm, which suggests he felt blamed and irritated, and he wondered whether it was really an apology. He kept his voice steady, so he may also have wanted to fix it.

qa.q: What did Tejas do that helped?
qa.a: He calmly asked Hrithik to say the sorry without the added complaint, then moved the harder conversation somewhere quiet.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see his first attempt?
qa.a: He may have thought he was being fair by naming both sides, without realising it sounded like blame.

grounding: A conditional non-apology is spotted and turned into a plain apology.

passage: The yearbook photographer was hurrying through Class Ten with ten minutes left before the bell, and everyone was crowding together. Rukmini stepped back from the group. "I'd rather not be in a close pose today. I don't like being squeezed." Aparna, next to her, nodded. "Okay. Stand at the end, then, we'll leave a gap." A boy at the back called out, "Come on, just squash in," and reached for her sleeve. Rukmini pulled her arm away and said clearly, "I said no." Aparna raised her hand. "Sir, she's said no." The teacher stopped the boy and moved Rukmini to the side. Afterwards Rukmini thanked Aparna quietly and told the teacher she would like to talk about the boy.

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the bell?
qa.a: Ten minutes were left before the bell.

qa.q: What does Rukmini's step back and steady voice show about how she felt?
qa.a: It shows she was uncomfortable with being squeezed and wanted her preference respected. Her later request to talk to the teacher suggests she was also bothered by the boy.

qa.q: What should Rukmini do if someone keeps ignoring her refusal?
qa.a: Keep saying no, stay near people who support her and tell a trusted adult, as she did with the teacher.

qa.q: How might Aparna have felt when the boy reached for Rukmini's sleeve?
qa.a: She may have felt alarmed and protective, which is why she raised her hand and spoke to Sir.

grounding: A teen states a preference about touch and photos, expects it respected and tells a trusted adult when it is ignored.

passage:
Shreya kept her voice even. "Nazia, can you not touch my hair? I don't like it."
"Sorry!" Nazia pulled her hand back. "I was only playing with the ribbon."
"I know. It's just not something I like."
"Okay. Thanks for telling me."
At the bus stop, Yash from the next class tugged Shreya's ponytail and grinned. "Come on, it's a joke." Shreya said, "I said stop. I don't like it." He did it again. Her stomach dropped. Nazia stepped between them and said, "She told you no." That evening Shreya told her aunt, who said she'd talk to the school. Shreya felt tired but lighter.

qa.q: What did Shreya ask Nazia not to touch?
qa.a: She asked Nazia not to touch her hair.

qa.q: What did Shreya feel when Yash pulled her ponytail again?
qa.a: Her stomach dropped, which suggests fear or alarm after her no was ignored. She may also have felt embarrassed in front of others.

qa.q: What worked well in how Nazia responded, twice?
qa.a: At first she stopped at once and thanked Shreya for telling her, and later she stood between Shreya and Yash and repeated that Shreya had said no.

qa.q: How might Yash see his ponytail tugging?
qa.a: He may think it is harmless teasing, but a no from Shreya means he should stop whatever his intent.

grounding: A teen states preferences about touch, a friend respects it, and a refusal ignored by another is brought to a trusted adult.

subtype: Hiding needs to avoid burdening others [Regulating]
passage: Pema's "I'm fine" was the third one I'd heard that morning, and I sit right next to her, so I noticed. Her eyes looked heavy and she had barely touched her tiffin at recess. When Ms Rao asked who could stay after school to help with the stage, Pema said yes before anyone else, and she smiled quickly. I don't know why she said yes. Maybe she wanted to be useful, or feared saying no would look lazy. At the gate I said, "You seem really tired. Do you want to skip the staying and just go home? I can tell Ms Rao." She looked at me a bit surprised, then whispered, "Actually, yes." Ira.

qa.q: How many times had Ira heard Pema say she was fine that morning?
qa.a: She had heard it three times.

qa.q: What might Pema have been feeling when she volunteered to stay?
qa.a: She may have felt tired but afraid of seeming lazy or needy. Ira admits she does not know for sure and that Pema might just have wanted to help.

qa.q: What did Ira do that made it easier for Pema to say what she needed?
qa.a: She named what she saw without judgement, offered to tell the teacher and let Pema choose.

qa.q: How might Ms Rao see Pema's quick yes?
qa.a: She likely took it at face value, as a keen student, since Pema smiled and showed no sign of trouble.

grounding: A teen says she is fine while tired, and a classmate notices the withdrawal.

subtype: Hiding needs to avoid burdening others [Regulating]
passage:
Monday. At football practice Bhupen said "I'm fine" when Coach asked why he was so quiet. His friend Alka looked at his bag: he had skipped lunch again and his hands were unsteady on the ball.
Wednesday. Alka waited by the gate and said, "You've been carrying a lot. What do you need? Even one thing." Bhupen said, "I didn't want to be a bother. I just need to eat properly and sleep before the test."
Friday. Bhupen walked up to Coach himself: "I've been overwhelmed. Can I sit out half the practice today?" Coach said yes. Bhupen felt lighter afterwards, and he told Alka thanks.

qa.q: What did Bhupen say when the coach asked why he was quiet?
qa.a: He said, "I'm fine."

qa.q: Why did Bhupen not tell anyone how he was really feeling at first?
qa.a: He did not want to be a bother, which suggests he worried about seeming needy. He may also have been too tired to explain himself.

qa.q: What small step helped Bhupen on Friday?
qa.a: He plainly told Coach he was overwhelmed and asked to sit out half the practice, so the small problem did not grow.

qa.q: How might the coach see Bhupen's request?
qa.a: He may be relieved that Bhupen said it, and glad to understand why he had been quiet. 🙂

grounding: A teen hides needs to avoid burdening others, then learns to state them plainly.

passage: In their flat in Hamburg, Ingrid closed her bedroom door a little harder than she meant. Her father Rafael knocked twice. "Everything okay?" "I want to be alone, please," she said. "Stop asking me questions." It came out blunter than she wanted. Rafael stood outside for a moment, feeling something small and sad, then remembered it wasn't about him. He said through the door, "Okay. I'll be in the kitchen. Would ten minutes and a cup of tea after dinner work for a check-in?" A long pause. "Yeah. After dinner is fine." At eight o'clock she came out with her sketchbook and said, "Thanks for waiting," and sat beside him without a word.

qa.q: In which city was the flat?
qa.a: The flat was in Hamburg.

qa.q: What did Ingrid seem to need when she closed her bedroom door?
qa.a: She seemed to need quiet and time to sort out her thoughts alone, and her bluntness was probably not directed at her father. She might also have been upset about something she was not ready to talk about.

qa.q: What did Rafael do that balanced respect and care?
qa.a: He stepped away and proposed a short check-in after dinner, so Ingrid had space and knew he was available.

qa.q: How might Rafael have felt outside the door?
qa.a: He felt something small and sad, which suggests he was a little hurt, yet he reminded himself it was not about him. 🙂

grounding: A teen bluntly asks for space and privacy, and a parent respects it with an agreed check-in.

passage: The hostel corridor smelled of talcum powder and wet towels. On Thursday evening Charu put her headphones on, pulled her curtain and said to her roommate Lavanya, "I need the room quiet tonight. Please don't ask me what's wrong." Lavanya raised her eyebrows. "Did I do something?" "No. I just need to be alone with my head." Lavanya took her book to the common room and left a chocolate wrapper folded on Charu's pillow with the word 'here' written on it. Around nine, Charu came out and sat beside her. "Thanks. I had a bad call with Papa. I didn't want to talk about it, but I do a little now." Lavanya moved her book aside.

qa.q: What did Charu pull before asking for quiet?
qa.a: She pulled her curtain.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she told Lavanya not to ask what was wrong?
qa.a: She probably felt upset and needed time alone to think, which was about processing and not about rejecting Lavanya. Later she says she had a bad call with her father.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do that helped?
qa.a: She took her book to the common room to give space and left a small note that showed she was there if Charu wanted her.

qa.q: What might Lavanya have wondered when Charu asked for space?
qa.a: She wondered whether she had done something wrong, and Charu's reassurance helped her relax.

grounding: A teen asks bluntly for space, and a roommate respects it while showing she is available.

passage: The group poster for the history project was due Monday, and Anand had drawn most of it. Disha studied the timeline he had drawn and took a breath. Last week she had snapped at him, "You're useless at layouts," and he'd gone silent for two days. Today she said instead, "The dates on the left are hard to read. Could we make them bigger?" Anand's shoulders tightened first, then loosened. "Yeah, I rushed that part," he said. "Show me which ones?" She pointed to three dates. He fixed them in ten minutes and asked, "Anything else unclear?" Disha shook her head. "No, the rest works. I like the colours." They pinned it to the wall.

qa.q: What was due on Monday?
qa.a: The group poster for the history project was due Monday.

qa.q: How did Anand feel at first when Disha pointed out the dates?
qa.a: His shoulders tightened first, which suggests he felt a flash of defensiveness, and then he loosened when he saw she was talking about the dates, not about him.

qa.q: Which of Disha's two comments was more useful, and why?
qa.a: Saying the dates are hard to read gave him a specific thing to fix, while calling him useless gave him nothing to fix and only hurt.

qa.q: How might Anand have felt during the two days of silence last week?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and discouraged, and afraid that any drawing he did would be attacked.

grounding: Criticism aimed at the act is usable, and feedback is accepted without collapsing or attacking.

passage: "That paragraph doesn't make sense," Minakshi said, tapping Bhavna's essay. "Which part?" Bhavna asked, gripping her pencil. "The second line. I can't tell who 'they' is." Bhavna groaned. "I'm so bad at this." Minakshi shook her head. "You're not. I'm saying that line is unclear, not that you are. Should I read it aloud so we can hear it?" Bhavna nodded. As Minakshi read, Bhavna said, "Oh, I meant the villagers. I wrote 'they' too early." She fixed it. Then she added, "Can you tell me when something works too? I only hear the bad parts." Minakshi laughed. "The last paragraph made me smile."

qa.q: What did Minakshi say was unclear?
qa.a: She said the second line was unclear, because she could not tell who 'they' is.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna say she was bad at writing?
qa.a: She seemed to feel stung and to take the comment about the line as being about her, which is a common reaction to criticism. Her tight grip on her pencil shows her tension.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do that made her feedback easier to use?
qa.a: She pointed to one line, said the line was unclear and not her, and offered to read it aloud together.

qa.q: What would you advise Bhavna to do when she hears feedback next time?
qa.a: Ask which part it refers to, as she did, and ask for what works too.

grounding: Constructive criticism targets the plan, and the writer receives it without collapsing.

passage: Everyone in my class thought I was being dramatic when I rolled my eyes at the new rule. The school had banned phones in the canteen and started handing out detention slips, and nobody asked us. I sighed loudly every recess for a week. I stopped eating with the girls and stared out of the window. My friend Farida said, "You're just being a brat." That hurt more than the rule. Later I understood I wasn't angry at the rule as much as at not being heard. So I wrote a polite letter with three reasons and twenty signatures and gave it to the principal. She didn't cancel the rule, but she agreed to meet a student group. Deepika.

qa.q: What did the school ban in the canteen?
qa.a: The school banned phones in the canteen.

qa.q: What was Deepika really upset about besides the rule?
qa.a: She realised she was mostly angry that nobody asked the students, so she wanted to be heard and respected. Her sighing and silence hid that wish.

qa.q: What did Deepika do that worked better than sighing?
qa.a: She wrote a polite letter with reasons and signatures and gave it to the principal, who agreed to meet a student group.

qa.q: How might Farida have seen Deepika's eye-rolls?
qa.a: She may have seen them as sulking or attitude, since she could not see what was underneath. 🙂

grounding: A teen protests a rule with eye-rolls and sighs, and a respectful channel gets a hearing.

passage: Coach's note, Thursday. Dolma led about fifteen students to the gate at lunch with a hand-lettered sign: 'Keep the library open till 6.' They stood quietly on the side without blocking anyone. Some rolled their eyes and sighed at the staff, and one boy got loud. Dolma pulled him aside and reminded him about their plan. I watched from the pitch. I wondered if the protest was about the library hours or about wanting to be listened to, and her face suggested a bit of both. I asked her to send her request in writing to the principal, and I offered to attach my support. She said, "Thank you, sir." Sahil, sports coach.

qa.q: What did Dolma's sign say?
qa.a: Her sign said, 'Keep the library open till 6.'

qa.q: What might Dolma be feeling and wanting behind the protest?
qa.a: She seems to want the library to stay open and to have students' voices heard, and Sahil thinks it may be a bit of both. She also acted responsibly by calming the loud boy.

qa.q: What could Dolma do next to make the protest effective?
qa.a: Send a written request to the principal with the coach's support and keep the group peaceful and respectful.

qa.q: How might a teacher watching the gate feel about the protest?
qa.a: They may feel challenged or worried about disruption, or they may respect the calm way the students went about it.

grounding: A teen joins a peaceful protest, and respectful channels are more effective than escalation.

passage: "You always take my charger!" Akash's voice was rising. Jahnavi, his sister, put the laptop down. "I did not. You lost it yourself!" "Liar!" His hands were shaking. She saw his jaw clench and felt her own heartbeat quicken. She took a breath. "Akash, I'm getting loud. Let's stop. I'll talk to you in fifteen minutes, okay?" "Why, so you can get out of it?" "No. Because I'll say something I don't mean." She walked to the balcony and looked at the traffic. When she came back, he was sitting on the sofa with the charger in his hand, found under his pillow. "Sorry," he muttered. "Thanks for waiting."

qa.q: Where did Jahnavi go to calm down?
qa.a: She went to the balcony.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi afraid might happen if they kept arguing?
qa.a: She felt her heartbeat quicken and worried she would say something she did not mean, which is why she stopped. She was also angry, but did not want to hurt him.

qa.q: What worked in how Jahnavi handled the argument?
qa.a: She named that she was getting loud, proposed talking later and stepped away, which let both of them cool down.

qa.q: How might Akash have read Jahnavi walking away at first?
qa.a: He may have thought she was avoiding the argument, until she came back and he found the charger. 🙂

grounding: A teen lowers her voice, pauses and steps away from a heated argument.

passage: The argument with Ankita about the group project got worse each minute. I could feel my face getting hot, and I heard my own voice rising, "You never do your part!" I saw her eyes fill with tears. I remembered what Mr Fernandes taught us in class: notice the heat, then pause. I said, "Ankita, I'm too angry to talk well. Let's talk later." I picked up my bag and went to the water cooler and drank slowly. Some friends thought I was running away. But when I came back after lunch, we could speak in quiet voices, and I admitted I had exaggerated. I'm Francis, and I learned that cooling down is not the same as giving up.

qa.q: What did Francis say he was too angry to do?
qa.a: He said he was too angry to talk well.

qa.q: What did Francis feel in himself that told him to pause, and what might he have worried about?
qa.a: His face was getting hot and his voice was rising, which he read as a sign he was too angry to talk well. He may also have been afraid of hurting Ankita.

qa.q: What would you advise Francis if the anger comes back later?
qa.a: Say he needs a pause, step away, drink water or breathe, and return when calmer to talk.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt when Francis left?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt or confused at first, but on his return she could speak calmly.

grounding: A teen steps away from a heated argument and returns to talk later.

subtype: Insults, taunts and challenges among peers [Interpreting]
passage: Noor, when I was fifteen, and yes, this is your Hafsa khala talking, a boy named Pran said, in front of the whole bus, "Nice haircut, did you lose a bet?" Everyone laughed. I didn't know if he was joking, because he said it with a grin and we had teased each other for years. I looked at my friends. They were laughing at him too, so I laughed and said, "Yes, I lost to a goat." That was banter. But a month later a boy from another school sent nasty messages in a group chat and dared me to answer, again and again. That felt like an attack meant to provoke. I did not answer. I took screenshots and showed my mother, and the messages stopped.

qa.q: Where did Pran make the remark about the haircut?
qa.a: He made it on the bus, in front of everyone.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa feel the message from the boy from another school was different?
qa.a: The tone was nasty and repeated, and it came with dares to answer, which felt like an attempt to provoke a reaction. Pran's remark came with a grin and from an old friend.

qa.q: What protective steps did Hafsa take?
qa.a: She did not answer, saved screenshots and showed her mother.

qa.q: How might Pran have seen his joke on the bus?
qa.a: Probably as ordinary teasing between friends, though it may not have felt the same to everyone listening.

grounding: An elder tells how tone, history and audience separate banter from attack, and not answering and saving evidence protect.

subtype: Insults, taunts and challenges among peers [Interpreting]
passage: The bus was loud and the match on the driver's radio drowned out most of it. Bhavna's phone buzzed. In the class group, a boy had posted, 'Bet you can't score even one goal, Bhavna. Dare you to try in front of everyone.' A few laughing emojis followed. Minakshi, sitting next to her, leaned over. "Is this a joke or a shove?" Bhavna's cheeks burned. She looked at who sent it, remembered he had done this before, and noticed the crowd of watchers. "It's not friendly." She did not type a reply. Instead she took a screenshot and whispered, "Can you help me show this to Ma'am tomorrow?" Minakshi nodded and squeezed her hand.

qa.q: Whose phone buzzed on the bus?
qa.a: Bhavna's phone buzzed.

qa.q: What made Bhavna decide the message was not friendly?
qa.a: She looked at who sent it, remembered he had done this before and noticed the crowd watching, so it felt like a shove meant to provoke her. Her burning cheeks show it hurt.

qa.q: What steps did Bhavna take that protect her?
qa.a: She did not reply, she took a screenshot and asked Minakshi to help show it to Ma'am.

qa.q: How might the boy who posted it see the message?
qa.a: He may say he was only joking, but the past pattern and the audience suggest it was meant to provoke.

grounding: A teen reads tone, history and audience to see an online taunt as an attack, and does not reply but saves evidence.
